questions.q: What happens if a deep network's weights are initialized with values that are too large?
options: Nothing; PyTorch automatically rescales weights during the first forward pass
Activation values (and the gradients computed from them) can grow uncontrollably, or 'explode', as they pass through successive layers
The model trains faster but less accurately
The optimizer automatically switches from Adam to SGD
questions.explain: Too-large initial weights cause each layer's output variance to grow relative to its input, compounding across layers and potentially causing activations and gradients to explode to very large values before training even meaningfully begins.

questions.q: Why is nn.init.kaiming_uniform_ specifically well-suited to networks using ReLU activations?
options: It initializes all weights to exactly zero
Its derivation accounts for the fact that ReLU zeros out roughly half of its inputs, unlike Xavier initialization which assumes Sigmoid/Tanh-style activations
It is the only initialization scheme PyTorch provides
It only works on GPU tensors
questions.explain: Kaiming (He) initialization was derived specifically with ReLU's behavior in mind -- since ReLU zeroes out negative inputs, roughly halving the active signal, Kaiming's scaling compensates for that in a way Xavier's does not.

questions.q: What does the trailing underscore in a function name like nn.init.xavier_uniform_ indicate, following PyTorch convention?
options: The function is deprecated
The function modifies its input tensor in place rather than returning a new tensor
The function only works with integer tensors
The function requires a GPU
questions.explain: PyTorch's convention is that a trailing underscore marks an in-place operation. nn.init.xavier_uniform_ modifies the passed-in weight tensor directly rather than returning a separately allocated new tensor.

questions.q: What does model.apply(init_weights) do, where init_weights is a function checking isinstance(module, nn.Linear)?
options: It calls init_weights only on the top-level model object
It recursively calls init_weights on every submodule in the model, and the isinstance check ensures only nn.Linear layers get re-initialized, skipping layers like nn.ReLU that have no weight
It raises an error because nn.Module has no apply method
It permanently disables gradient tracking on the model
questions.explain: model.apply(fn) walks the entire submodule tree, recursively calling fn on each one -- the same tree-walking mechanism that powers .parameters(). The isinstance check is necessary because apply visits every submodule, not just the ones with weights to initialize.

questions.q: Why don't most beginners need to think about weight initialization when first using nn.Linear?
options: Because weight initialization has no effect on training in modern PyTorch
Because nn.Linear already initializes its weight and bias with a reasonable default (a Kaiming-uniform-derived scheme) automatically, without any extra code
Because nn.Linear layers start with all weights equal to zero, which is always fine
Because initialization only matters for convolutional layers
questions.explain: PyTorch's nn.Linear performs sensible default initialization automatically upon construction, which is adequate for many networks -- it's only as architectures get deeper or use particular activation functions that overriding this default becomes worthwhile.
